## What are we measuring?

![Image courtesy of Data Carpentry](/assets/01_alternative_splicing.png) <!-- why isn't this working??? {fig-alt="A diagram illustrating the biological process of alternative splicing. The top level depicts a DNA double helix with five color-coded exons (labeled Exon 1 through Exon 5) separated by intervening sequences. The middle level shows a single-stranded primary RNA transcript containing the corresponding five exons. Arrows pointing downward labeled "Alternative Splicing" lead to the bottom level, which displays three distinct mature mRNA molecules generated by combining the exons in different ways: the first transcript contains all five exons (1, 2, 3, 4, 5), the second transcript skips exon 3 (containing 1, 2, 4, 5), and the third transcript skips exon 4 (containing 1, 2, 3, 5)."}-->

::: {.content-visible when-profile="notes"}
To start off with, let's review what, exactly, we're measuring in an RNA-seq experiment.

In order to produce an RNA molecule, a stretch of DNA is first transcribed into mRNA. Subsequently, intronic regions are spliced out, and exonic regions are combined into different isoforms of a gene.

> `<refer to introns>`

These regions are called introns, and they get discarded during the creation of messenger RNA - you'll often see this written as mRNA - then the final mRNA that we'll be measuring is made up of one or more exons, spliced together.
:::

### Data generation

![Figure adapted from @martin_next-generation_2011](/assets/01_rnaseq_martin_wang.png)

::: {.content-visible when-profile="notes"}
In a typical RNA-seq experiment, RNA molecules are first collected from a sample of interest.

After a potential enrichment for molecules with polyA tails (predominantly mRNA), or depletion of otherwise highly abundant ribosomal RNA, the remaining molecules are fragmented into smaller pieces (there are also long-read protocols where entire molecules are considered, but those are not the focus of this lesson).

As we saw in the last slide, the splicing excluding intronic sequences results in an RNA molecule that may not correspond to an uninterrupted region of the genome.

The RNA fragments are reverse transcribed into cDNA, whereafter sequencing adapters are added to each end.

These adapters allow the fragments to attach to the flow cell, that will eventually be read by the machine. Once they attach, each fragment will be heavily amplified to generate a cluster of identical sequences on the flow cell.

The sequencer then determines the sequence of the first 50-200 nucleotides of the cDNA fragments in each such cluster, starting from one end. This corresponds to a read that we will get in our fastq output.

Many data sets are generated with paired-end protocols, where fragments are read from both ends.

Millions of these reads (or pairs of reads) will be generated in an experiment, and these will be represented in a FASTQ file - or a pair of files.

Each read is represented by four consecutive lines in such a file:

-   first, a line with a unique read identifier
-   next, the inferred sequence of the read
-   then another identifier line, and
-   finally a line containing the base quality for each inferred nucleotide - this quality score represents the probability that the nucleotide at the corresponding position has been correctly identified.
:::

#### Paired-end vs Single-end reads

![Image courtesy of [Illumina](https://www.illumina.com/science/technology/next-generation-sequencing/plan-experiments/paired-end-vs-single-read.html)](/assets/01_paired-end-vs-single-read-seq-web-graphic.jpg)

::: {.content-visible when-profile="notes"}
Paired-end sequencing reads both the 5' and 3' ends of each cDNA fragment, whereas single-end sequencing reads only one direction. The choice between paired-end and single-end determines mapping accuracy, isoform resolution, computational overhead, and experimental budget allocation.

Some advantages of paired-end sequencing include:

-   Transcript Isoform & Splicing Resolution
    -   A cDNA fragment of 250–350 bp sequenced from both ends can anchor one read in an upstream exon and the mate in an alternative downstream exon. This physical linkage not only proves that the two exons coexist in the same mature mRNA molecule, but it also gives us an idea about how far apart they are.
    -   Also, transcript-level abundance estimation tools (such as Salmon, Kallisto, and RSEM) perform EM-algorithm deconvolution of multi-isoform genes with significantly lower variance when you use paired-end reads.
-   Another advantage is disambiguation of repetitive regions
    -   When Read 1 falls into a repeat element, read 2 often lands in unique flanking sequence.
    -   Aligners like STAR and HISAT2 use the expected insert-size distribution to reject spurious mapping loci. This can turn what would be multi-mapped or discarded single-end reads into uniquely aligned reads.
-   Paired-end reads can also help with
    -   Detection of gene fusions and structural variants, and
    -   *De Novo* transcriptome assembly

There are some disadvantages to think about as well.

-   The main disadvantage is cost.
    -   Sequencing both ends roughly doubles the cycle count, which increases sequencing reagent costs by 50% to 100% per flow cell lane.
    -   When we factor budget considerations into the planning equation, the question often comes down to: do we peform paired-end sequencing, or do we include more biological replicates?
-   For standard differential gene expression (DGE) in well-annotated model organisms like human or mouse, single-end reads map to unique gene loci with \>85–90% efficiency. This results in a diminishing returns scenario if your main question is gene expression - as opposed to isoform identification, for example.
    -   From a statistical standpoint, statistical power to detect differential gene expression is driven far more by the number of biological replicates than by paired-end resolution. For example, single-end sequencing of 6 biological replicates yields superior statistical power compared to 3 biological replicates with paired-end sequence for roughly the same total expenditure.
-   There is also the issue of fragment length. If your cDNA fragments are shorter than twice the read length, the sequencer reads through into the opposite adapter. This isn't a show stopper, but it requires agressive adapter trimming and quality control.
:::

## Experimental design considerations

![Image courtesy of @lazic_experimental_2016](/assets/01_factors-affecting-measurements.png)

::: {.content-visible when-profile="notes"}
Before starting to collect data, it is essential to take some time to think about the design of the experiment.

Experimental design helps us organize the experiment with the purpose of making sure that the right type of data, and enough of it, is available to answer the questions of interest - and we want to do that as efficiently as possible.

Aspects such as

-   which conditions or sample groups to consider
-   how many replicates to collect, and
-   how to collect the data

are important questions to consider.

Many high-throughput biological experiments (including RNA-seq) are sensitive to ambient conditions, and it is often difficult to directly compare measurements that have been done on different days, by different analysts, in different centers, or using different batches of reagents.

For this reason, it is very important to design experiments properly, to make it possible to disentangle different types of (primary and secondary) effects.
:::

#### Discussion

::: {.content-visible when-profile="notes"}
Time for another discussion. Take a minute to discuss the following questions with the chat bot provided below.
:::

-   Why is it essential to have replicates?

::: {.content-visible when-profile="notes"}
> `<cut to next video>`

Welcome back! So, why is it essential to have replicates? We touched on a few of the reasons an an earlier video, but not all replicates are equally useful, from a statistical point of view.

One common way to classify the different types of replicates is as 'biological' and 'technical'.

-   Technical replicates are typically used to test the *reproducibility of the measurement device* - for example measuring batch effects and accounting for them - while
-   biological replicates inform us about the variability *between different samples* from a population of interest - this usually applies direclty to the scientific questions we are trying to answer.

Replication of biological units is required to make a general statement of the effect of a treatment - we can't draw a conclusion about the effect of drug on a population of mice by studying a single mouse only. Sometimes there are additional experimental units that need to be taken into consideration as well. For example,

-   Longitudinal measurements over time on an individual
-   Mouse pups from the same litter
-   Animals from the same cage
-   etc...
:::

## RNA-seq quantification

::: {.content-visible when-profile="slides"}
How do we get from raw reads to a count matrix?
:::

::: {.content-visible when-profile="notes"}
The raw read sequences contained in the FASTQ files from the sequencer are typically not directly useful as they are, since we don't have the information about which gene or transcript they originate from.

The first processing step is to attempt to identify the location of origin for each read, and use this to obtain an estimate of the number of reads that originate from each gene - or depending on the scientific question, another features, such as individual transcripts.

This can then be used as a proxy for the abundance, or expression level, of the gene.

There are lots of RNA quantification pipelines, and the most common approaches can be categorized into three main types:
:::

### Align reads to the genome

::: {.content-visible when-profile="notes"}
One of simplest methods. For species for which the transcriptome is poorly annotated, this would be the preferred approach.

First we align reads to the genome, then we
:::

-   Count the number of reads that map within the exons of each gene
-   Example: STAR

### Align reads to the transcriptome

::: {.content-visible when-profile="notes"}
Aligning reads to a transcriptome can produce accurate quantification results, particularly for high-quality samples without DNA contamination.

In this case, we use the aligned reads to
:::

-   Quantify transcript expression
-   Summarize transcript expression into gene expression
-   Example: RSEM

### Pseudoalign reads against the transcriptome

::: {.content-visible when-profile="slides"}
-   Quantify transcript expression
-   Summarize the transcript-level expression into gene-level expression
-   Example: salmon
:::

::: {.content-visible when-profile="notes"}
Pseudo alignment uses the corresponding genome as a decoy and quantifies transcript expression and summarizes expression into gene-level expression.

The output is similar to the alignment we discussed in the previous slide.

The advantages of this approach include:

-   computational efficiency
-   mitigation of the effect of DNA contamination, and
-   GC bias correction

This is the approach implented by salmon.
:::

### Other software

::: {.content-visible when-profile="notes"}
At typical sequencing read depth, gene expression quantification is often more accurate than transcript expression quantification. However, differential gene expression analyses can be improved by having access also to transcript-level quantifications.

Other tools commonly used in RNA-seq quantification include:
:::

-   TopHat2
-   bowtie2
-   kallisto
-   HTseq

::: {.content-visible when-profile="notes"}
The choice of an appropriate RNA-seq quantification depends on

-   the quality of the transcriptome annotation
-   the quality of the RNA-seq library preparation
-   the presence of contaminating sequences, and
-   many other factors

Often, it can be informative to compare the quantification results of multiple approaches - especially in the age of AI agents, where running multiple versions of an anlysis is more feasible.

Because the best quantification method is species- and experiment-dependent, and often requires large amounts of computing resources, this series will not cover the specifics of how to generate the counts.
:::

## Finding reference sequences

::: {.content-visible when-profile="notes"}
In order to quantify abundances of known genes or transcripts from RNA-seq data, we need a reference database informing us of the sequence of these features, to which we can then compare our reads.

This information can be obtained from different online repositories.

It is highly recommended to choose one of these for a particular project, and not mix information from different sources.

Depending on the quantification tool you have chosen, you will need different types of reference information. If you are aligning your reads to the genome and investigating the overlap with known annotated features, you will need the full genome sequence (provided in a fasta file) and a file that tells you the genomic location of each annotated feature (typically provided in a gtf file).

If you are mapping your reads to a transcriptome, you will instead need a file with the sequence of each transcript (again, a fasta file).
:::

-   If you are working with mouse or human samples, the [GENCODE project](https://www.gencodegenes.org/) provides well-curated reference files.

-   [Ensembl](https://www.ensembl.org/info/data/ftp/index.html) provides reference files for a large set of organisms, including [plants](https://plants.ensembl.org/info/data/ftp/index.html) and [fungi](https://fungi.ensembl.org/info/data/ftp/index.html).

-   [UCSC](https://hgdownload.soe.ucsc.edu/downloads.html) also provides reference files for many organisms.

Let's go ahead and take a look at this file in R. First I need to load `Biostrings`

```R
library(Biostrings)
```

And if you don't have that installed, you can do that with the `BiocManager` package. The commands you'll need are

```R
install.packages('BiocManager')

```

Once we have that loaded, I am going to read in our fasta file with

```R
mouse_tx <- readDNAStringSet('gencode.vM39.transcripts.fa.gz')
```

> start loading while I talk

Also, as I mentioned before, this isn't exactly a small file. Most systems should be able to handle it, but if yours can't try opening it up on a computer with more memory.

When we print this out to the screen, we can see that it has around 480 thousand sequences in the file. The Biostrings package has some nice visualization features, too, and includes the

-   Sequence length
-   Beginning and end of each sequence, and
-   Name associated with each of them - these particular names are not very human readable, but they are great for our code. We'll work on annotation at a later point.

## Looking forward

:::{.content-visible when-profile="notes"}
Throughout the following videos in this series, we will discuss and practice how to perform differential expression analysis with Bioconductor, and how to interpret the results.

We will start from a count matrix, and thus assume that the initial quality assessment and quantification of gene expression have already been done.

The outcome of a differential expression analysis is often represented using graphical representations, such as MA plots and heatmaps.
:::

![Example MA plot](/assets/01_maPlot-example.png)

:::{.content-visible when-profile="notes"}
This MA plot, for example, shows us the mean of normalized counts on the x-axis - that is, counts are averaged over all samples - and log fold change between our groups of interest on the y-axis.

The blue points represent genes that are significantly differentially expressed.

If we are comparing a treatment group to a controll group, these points at the top are much more highly expressed in the treatment group, and these points at the bottom are much more highly expressed in the control group.
:::

:::{.content-visible when-profile="slides"}
## Looking forward
:::

![Example heat map](/assets/01_heatmap-example.png)

:::{.content-visible when-profile="notes"}
In this example heatmap, we have the top 10 most differentially expressed genes, showing expression for each individual - with up-regulated genes being more red and down-regulated genes being more blue.

We can look at patterns over time and sex of the individuals to identify groups of genes where expression patterns correlate with different categories - time and sex in this case.

In the following videos we will learn, among other things, how to generate and interpret these plots. It is also common to perform follow-up analyses to investigate whether there is a functional relationship among the top-ranked genes - this is called a gene set (enrichment) analysis.
:::
